bivy.name: The Bench
SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
bivy.notes: THIS IS THE HONEST ANSWER FOR MOST OBJECTIVES HERE: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
bivy.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
bivy.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
bivy.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
bivy.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
bivy.water: Developed campgrounds with seasonal water systems; all three also sit on or near creeks. Water is shut off outside the operating season.
bivy.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

bivy.name: Kangaroo Pass and the upper Early Winters Creek meadows
bivy.notes: The approach from the hairpin is short enough that camping up here is widely DISCOURAGED rather than encouraged, and many parties say so plainly: the meadows and the pass take damage quickly and most parties simply do Kangaroo Temple in a day. Some do carry up and sleep near the tarn to get an early start on a longer link-up, so the practice exists even though it is not recommended. If you go, use bare ground well away from the meadow and expect the tarn to be a dry hollow after midsummer. Elevation figures for the pass are not consistently reported, so plan on a cold, exposed camp rather than a specific number.
bivy.water: A small tarn below the pass is the only source and it commonly dries out by late summer and autumn. Treat it as unreliable and carry water from the road.
bivy.permit: None required — Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any quota area. Leave-no-trace practice is the only constraint, and it is a real one here.
bivy.capacity: A few small parties at most, on the flats south of the pass; the ground is fragile

bivy.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside parking
bivy.notes: Parties climbing the Liberty Bell group frequently sleep here, and it works as a fallback for the Kangaroo Ridge and roadside objectives when the hairpin lot is full, since it is only a few minutes' drive west. Be clear on the distinction: sleeping in the lot is tolerated, but walking up and pitching a tent at the lake is not. There is no water source you can rely on at the parking area.

bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park. No overnight backcountry permit and no reservation — this is national forest, not a North Cascades park camping zone. Overnight camping is prohibited within a quarter mile of Blue Lake.
bivy.capacity: A moderate paved lot that fills early on weekends; overnight use is vehicle-based only

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground
bivy.notes: The closest developed campground to Washington Pass, on SR 20 along Early Winters Creek six or seven miles east of the pass, just past the turn for the Cutthroat Creek road. Because nothing here can be booked, arriving Friday evening in July or August is a gamble and the fallback is dispersed camping on a spur road. The season runs roughly May or June through September or October, entirely dependent on when the highway opens and when snow returns.
bivy.water: Potable water provided in season, shut off once the campground closes for the year.

bivy.capacity: 27 sites, tents and small RVs

bivy.name: Klipchuck Campground, with Early Winters nearby
bivy.notes: Klipchuck sits about a quarter mile off SR 20 in fir and pine down-valley toward Mazama, low enough to be warm and dry when the passes are still wet. bivy.permit: First-come, first-served, nightly fee, no reservation and no permit required.
bivy.capacity: 46 sites, the largest campground on this stretch of highway

bivy.name: Cutthroat basin climbers' bivy, south side
bivy.notes: Serves every route reached through the basin south of the peak: the South and Complete South Buttress, the Southeast Buttress, the East Face lines over the rib, and the North Ridge by its usual approach, which bears right out of the same basin toward the North Ridge Notch. The way in starts from the long pullout on the north side of SR 20 about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass, not from the Cutthroat Lake trail on the east side of the pass: a cairned track leaves the pullout's east end, drops through timber to cross State Creek, and climbs meadows into the bowl, roughly two hours with a pack. Parties camp here to take a long route in a single push rather than commit to a headlamp descent. Ground is a mix of heather bench and talus and the pads are small, so a large party will be split up. The meadows are thin and the basin sees enough traffic to show it.
bivy.water: A snow-fed stream runs through the basin and usually carries water through the climbing season, but it thins as the snow patches under the peak melt out, which is why State Creek, low on the approach, is the last water to count on. Fill there, and carry enough for a dry night late in a hot summer.

bivy.capacity: Several scattered one- and two-tent pads in the meadows and among the boulders; no established camp, so parties spread out

bivy.notes: The lot sits a mile up the forest road from SR 20 and has a vault toilet but no water. bivy.water: None — no potable water at the trailhead. Cutthroat Creek runs below the lot and needs filtering.

bivy.capacity: Large gravel lot, roughly 20-30 vehicles; fills on summer weekends with larch-season hikers

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground
bivy.notes: The closest developed campground to Washington Pass, on SR 20 along Early Winters Creek six or seven miles east of the pass, just past the turn for the Cutthroat Creek road. Because nothing here can be booked, arriving Friday evening in July or August is a gamble and the fallback is dispersed camping on a spur road. The season runs roughly May or June through September or October, entirely dependent on when the highway opens and when snow returns.
bivy.water: Potable water provided in season, shut off once the campground closes for the year.
bivy.permit: No reservations and no permit — first-come, first-served with a nightly fee. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to camp, only to park at the trailhead.
bivy.capacity: 27 sites, tents and small RVs

bivy.name: Klipchuck Campground, with Early Winters nearby
bivy.notes: Klipchuck sits about a quarter mile off SR 20 in fir and pine down-valley toward Mazama, low enough to be warm and dry when the passes are still wet. Early Winters Campground is further east, smaller at around a dozen tent sites, split by the highway near the Methow River, and fills quickly. Both are a longer drive to the trailhead than Lone Fir, which is the tradeoff for a better chance of finding a site on a busy weekend.
bivy.water: Drinking water spigots in season; vault toilets. Water is turned off at the end of the season while the sites stay usable.
bivy.permit: First-come, first-served, nightly fee, no reservation and no permit required.
bivy.capacity: 46 sites, the largest campground on this stretch of highway

bivy.name: Cutthroat Wall base terrace
bivy.notes: The approach leaves the old roadbed a quarter mile from the trailhead at cairns, then climbs left through trees and light brush to a flat bench beneath the west-northwest-facing granite. The wall faces away from morning sun, which makes an early camp less useful than it looks on the map. The crag is sometimes catalogued under Little Liberty Bell, which is the same approach and the same ground.
bivy.water: No water on the terrace itself. Fill in Cutthroat Creek low on the approach and carry it up.
bivy.permit: None — dispersed national forest camping, no permit and no quota.
bivy.capacity: A small flat area under the cliff; room for one or two parties at most

bivy.water: Developed campgrounds with seasonal water systems; all three also sit on or near creeks. Water is shut off outside the operating season.
bivy.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

bivy.name: Kangaroo Pass and the upper Early Winters Creek meadows
bivy.notes: The approach from the hairpin is short enough that camping up here is widely DISCOURAGED rather than encouraged, and several parties say so plainly: the meadows and the pass take damage quickly and most parties simply do Kangaroo Temple in a day. Some do carry up and sleep near the tarn to get an early start on a longer link-up, so the practice exists even though it is not recommended. If you go, use bare ground well away from the meadow and expect the tarn to be a dry hollow after midsummer. Elevation figures for the pass are not consistently reported, so plan on a cold, exposed camp rather than a specific number.
bivy.water: A small tarn below the pass is the only source and it commonly dries out by late summer and autumn. Treat it as unreliable and carry water from the road.
bivy.permit: None required — Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any quota area. Leave-no-trace practice is the only constraint, and it is a real one here.
bivy.capacity: A few small parties at most, on the flats south of the pass; the ground is fragile

bivy.name: Bench Camp — larch bench above the Wine Spires pullout
bivy.notes: The one genuinely used high camp on the Kangaroo Ridge side, reached by a steep switchbacking climbers' trail that gains roughly 2,000 ft from the highway. It is the sensible base for Vasiliki Ridge and Vasiliki Tower, for the WEST side of Juno Tower, and for linking two or three routes over a weekend rather than re-walking the approach each morning. Juno's east-side routes are a different problem — a 2.5 to 3.5 hour approach with a valley camp in Silver Star Creek — and this camp does not serve them. Bugs can be bad in July; water availability is what actually varies.
bivy.water: Present early in the season from snowmelt and the creek drainage, but limited to non-existent by late summer and early autumn. Higher up, a tarn around 7,100 ft and year-round snow at Burgundy Col are the late-season backups.
bivy.permit: None — no reservation, no quota, no backcountry permit. Northwest Forest Pass for the vehicle at the pullout below.
bivy.capacity: Several established tent spots among the larches; the standard base for the north end of the ridge

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
bivy.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
bivy.water: Developed campgrounds with seasonal water systems; all three also sit on or near creeks. Water is shut off outside the operating season.
bivy.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

bivy.name: Cutthroat Creek trailhead
bivy.notes: The lot sits a mile up the forest road from SR 20 and has a vault toilet but no water. It is the start for Cutthroat Wall and for the Cutthroat Lake trail toward Cutthroat Pass, and some parties sleep here or in a pullout on the road in before a pre-dawn start, though the lot itself is signed for day use and how strictly that is read varies; dispersed camping in the trees along the forest road below is the uncontroversial option. Access is entirely gated by the SR 20 winter closure, and the road has been shut for construction windows in recent seasons, so confirm before driving out.
bivy.water: None — no potable water at the trailhead. Cutthroat Creek runs below the lot and needs filtering.
bivy.permit: No camping permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day pass covers parking. This is Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, NOT the national park, so there is no backcountry permit system here at all.
bivy.capacity: Large gravel lot, roughly 20-30 vehicles; fills on summer weekends with larch-season hikers

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground
bivy.notes: The closest developed campground to Washington Pass, on SR 20 along Early Winters Creek six or seven miles east of the pass, just past the turn for the Cutthroat Creek road. Because nothing here can be booked, arriving Friday evening in July or August is a gamble and the fallback is dispersed camping on a spur road. The season runs roughly May or June through September or October, entirely dependent on when the highway opens and when snow returns.
bivy.water: Potable water provided in season, shut off once the campground closes for the year.
bivy.permit: No reservations and no permit — first-come, first-served with a nightly fee. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to camp, only to park at the trailhead.
bivy.capacity: 27 sites, tents and small RVs

bivy.name: Klipchuck Campground, with Early Winters nearby
bivy.notes: Klipchuck sits about a quarter mile off SR 20 in fir and pine down-valley toward Mazama, low enough to be warm and dry when the passes are still wet. Early Winters Campground is further east, smaller at around a dozen tent sites, split by the highway near the Methow River, and fills quickly. Both are a longer drive to the trailhead than Lone Fir, which is the tradeoff for a better chance of finding a site on a busy weekend.
bivy.water: Drinking water spigots in season; vault toilets. Water is turned off at the end of the season while the sites stay usable.
bivy.permit: First-come, first-served, nightly fee, no reservation and no permit required.
bivy.capacity: 46 sites, the largest campground on this stretch of highway

bivy.name: Cutthroat Wall base terrace
bivy.notes: The approach leaves the old roadbed a quarter mile from the trailhead at cairns, then climbs left through trees and light brush to a flat bench beneath the west-northwest-facing granite. Most parties do these routes car-to-car in a day, so a bivy here is for a late start or a two-day plan rather than standard practice. The wall faces away from morning sun, which makes an early camp less useful than it looks on the map. The crag is sometimes catalogued under Little Liberty Bell, which is the same approach and the same ground.
bivy.water: No water on the terrace itself. Fill in Cutthroat Creek low on the approach and carry it up.
bivy.permit: None — dispersed national forest camping, no permit and no quota.
bivy.capacity: A small flat area under the cliff; room for one or two parties at most
